target_customer: Women working in or entering technology, plus sponsors and employers who funded programs and events
problem: Women in engineering lack community, mentoring and career support. Women Who Code ran chapters, events and leadership programs to address that.
business_model: Nonprofit funded by sponsorship, grants and event revenue

founders.name: Alaina Percival
founders.background_notes: YC page: led the organization to nearly half a million members in 147 countries; Venture Partner at Valor Ventures. Stepped down as CEO in January 2024 per press.

founders.name: Zassmin Montes de Oca
prior_employers: Coinbase (led security engineering, 2018 to 2022, after leaving the organization)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists her as co-founder, CTO and Board Vice Chair.

exit.reason: Board voted to dissolve the organization citing funding sources that had materially declined (announcement of 2024-04-18 as reported by press)

technical_complexity.rationale: A community and events organization with a website and meetup chapters; no hard technology.

defensibility.rationale: Large global chapter network and brand recognition among women technologists, but no proprietary asset and dependent on donors.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent tried to absorb it; it ended by dissolution in April 2024 for lack of funding.

market_need_then: In 2016 TechCrunch covered the YC acceptance as the second tech diversity nonprofit in YC; an August 2016 release reported over 80,000 members in 20 countries.

rebrands.to: Local groups such as Women and Gender eXpansive Coders (WGXC)
rebrands.why: Chapters kept going after the organization dissolved but needed a new name

branding.community_and_virality: Reported 360,000 technologists in 145 countries and more than 1,000 volunteers at closure; local chapters kept their Slack communities under new names.

brand_strength.rationale: Large global community and local groups that persisted under new names after closure, though the brand name closely resembles Girls Who Code.

outcome_analysis: Women Who Code grew into a large global community and joined YC in Summer 2016 as a nonprofit that received a charitable donation rather than giving equity. The founding CEO stepped down in January 2024 and the board voted in April 2024 to dissolve it, citing lost funding sources. The nonprofit model with intermittent grants and sponsor dependence left it exposed once funding fell, even with a strong brand and member base. The company website still operates in 2026, now focused on experienced technologists, and the directory status of Active conflicts with the 2024 dissolution.
notes: Directory status says Active but the organization announced dissolution on 2024-04-18 per its own blog and many outlets; the live website in 2026 describes a Summit 2027 and an experienced technologist focus, so a successor entity may operate under the same site (not confirmed). YC gave a charitable donation and took no stake per TechCrunch; amount not stated. A Craig Newmark Philanthropies grant exists per a company blog title, amount unread. Persana's claim of $150K across two rounds is unverified. No competitor sources dated near mid 2016 were opened; Girls Who Code, Girl Develop It and Black Girls Code are known peers only from undated pages. YC page founder education not given.
